opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
“It was not you who chose me, but I who chose you and appointed you to go and bear fruit that will remain.”

Something is mesmerizing about those words. Christ is not simply speaking to His disciples as followers. He is revealing something about the relationship between humanity, Himself, and the Father.

“You did not choose me.”

Humanity often believes it searched for God, reasoned toward God, and discovered God. Yet Christ says the movement began with Him first. “I chose you.”

Then later, He says He appointed humanity “to go and bear fruit that will remain.”

What actually remains?

Time consumes almost everything humanity builds. Empires collapse. Bodies age. Achievements fade. Even memory disappears with generations. Yet love somehow continues moving outward from person to person, generation to generation.

I sometimes think humanity is like pieces of a much larger picture. Alone, each piece can seem isolated or incomplete. Yet love becomes the thing that binds the pieces together into something whole. Those who truly love begin forming part of something beyond themselves, something stretching farther than individual lives or even nations. Scripture says the Gospel reaches to the ends of the Earth, but perhaps love itself reaches even farther than that — back to the Father from whom it came.

Maybe that is the fruit that remains.

Not simply what humanity builds or leaves behind, but love carried through humanity toward one another and ultimately back toward God. And if every act of genuine love joins itself back to the Father from whom it came, then perhaps Heaven is not merely a distant place waiting at the end of time, but a greater creation continuously expanding through love itself, almost parabolic in nature, always extending outward yet somehow returning to its source.
